Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Key clinical assessment (from transcript):
  - Unilateral (left) progressive hearing loss ~6 weeks.
  - Intermittent left-sided tinnitus.
  - Occasional mild dizziness/lightheadedness with some nausea (not true spinning vertigo).
  - No ear pain, no otorrhea/discharge, no documented fever, no chest pain or palpitations.
  - Prior short episode ~1 year ago.
  - Telehealth encounter only; no direct ear examination performed.
- Clinician impression and immediate plan from transcript:
  - Primary concern: exclude conductive causes such as cerumen impaction by performing otoscopic examination.
  - Plan: arrange face-to-face GP clinic appointment within ~4–5 days for ear exam; provide tinnitus information leaflet in notes; advise patient to contact support/admin to schedule; instructions to rebook if symptoms worsen.
- DDx integration (consistent with transcript):
  - Cerumen impaction / obstructive conductive hearing loss — High likelihood (clinician explicitly suspected this as an initial, common cause).
  - Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) — Moderate likelihood; consistent with unilateral progressive hearing loss + tinnitus and mild imbalance; warrants further workup if otoscopy normal.
  - Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis or otitis media with inner-ear involvement — Moderate likelihood; less likely given absence of pain/fever but still possible.
  - Meniere disease — Low–moderate likelihood; symptoms are not classic (dizziness not severe episodic vertigo).
- If otoscopy is normal, DDx-consistent next steps (not ordered yet but supported by DDx and clinician reasoning): consider audiometry and referral to ENT for further assessment and possible imaging (e.g., MRI) to evaluate for sensorineural causes such as vestibular schwannoma.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Cerumen (earwax) impaction / obstructive conductive hearing loss — High likelihood.
  - Justification: clinician explicitly suspected impacted wax as first-line cause; unilateral muffled hearing without pain/discharge; tinnitus may be masked by external sound; otoscopic exam will help confirm.
- Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: unilateral progressive hearing loss with unilateral tinnitus and mild imbalance fits pattern; less common than obstructive causes; consider audiometry/ENT referral and MRI if otoscopy and initial testing do not identify conductive cause.
- Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis or otitis media with inner-ear involvement — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: can present with unilateral hearing change, tinnitus and dizziness even without fever or severe pain; consider if otoscopy and initial testing do not reveal an obstructive cause.
